analysis.one_liner: Forces big credit card issuers to let merchants route transactions across competing payment networks.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on July 28, 2022 and never received a markup or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Large banks that issue credit cards (those with over $100 billion in assets) would no longer be allowed to send credit card transactions only to one or two payment networks, effectively the Visa and Mastercard duopoly. Merchants could choose a cheaper network to process each sale, which would put competitive pressure on the 'swipe fees' banks and networks charge stores every time a card is used. The rules would not apply to American Express and Discover, which issue their own cards, or to smaller issuers.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants who accept credit cards — from small shops to large chains — gain the right to route each transaction over any eligible network and avoid routing penalties, which would let them shop for lower processing fees. Consumers benefit indirectly and only if merchants pass their savings into lower prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Merchants, and consumers if savings pass through

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered issuers (those with over $100 billion in assets, including affiliates) from restricting transactions to a single network, to affiliated networks, or to only the two largest networks, opening routing to competing networks.
Bars issuers and networks from penalizing merchants for routing transactions over a network of their choice, including penalties for failing to meet volume thresholds on a particular network.
Requires the Federal Reserve to publish a list of payment card networks that pose a national security risk or are owned or sponsored by a foreign state entity.

analysis.who_pays: Visa, Mastercard, and the largest banks, which collect interchange (swipe) fees on every credit card transaction, would face competitive pressure on that revenue. Some of that loss could be shifted to cardholders through lower rewards or higher fees.

drawbacks.text: The mandate does not apply to three-party systems like American Express and Discover, which issue their own cards, leaving their fee structures untouched.

Savings to merchants are not guaranteed to reach consumers as lower prices; banks could also offset lost swipe-fee revenue by trimming rewards programs or raising annual fees, which would fall on cardholders. (General knowledge about how interchange revenue funds rewards; the bill text sets no pass-through requirement.

The rules apply only to issuers over $100 billion in assets, so smaller banks and credit unions are exempt, though their co-branded cards ride on the same networks and they argued they could still be squeezed. (Exemption supported by the bill text; the squeeze concern is widely reported industry argument.)

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core mechanism is real: routing competition is the only structural lever on credit card swipe fees, which are among the highest merchant costs in the payments system. But the benefit to ordinary shoppers is one step removed — it depends on merchants cutting prices — and the most likely offset is smaller rewards programs. The carve-outs for American Express, Discover, and banks under $100 billion narrow the bill to its true targets but also blunt its reach.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2022, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and sat there without a markup or floor vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Credit Card Competition Act of 2022 on July 28, 2022, with Sen. Marshall introducing it on his behalf as the single cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action appears in the record.
No version of the bill was reported out of committee or voted on by either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so it died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Visa, Mastercard, and the largest card-issuing banks keep the current routing rules and the swipe-fee revenue that comes with them; merchants keep paying the existing fees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Card networks and big banks kept status quo

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, building on his earlier debit-card routing mandate, to open credit card routing to competition.

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and introduced it on the floor on Durbin's behalf.

for.name: Merchant and retail coalitions (e.g., Merchants Payments Coalition, National Retail Federation)
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for Congress to pass credit routing competition to cut merchants' swipe fees.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee (Chair Sherrod Brown)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further recorded action — no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Electronic Payments Coalition (bank and card-network lobby)
against.role: Industry coalition of large banks and payment networks
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against routing mandates, arguing they would end rewards programs and shift costs to consumers and smaller banks.

against.name: Visa and Mastercard
against.role: The two dominant credit card networks
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, which directly targets the two largest networks' share of credit card routing; both spent heavily on lobbying against routing legislation.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor was joined by a single Republican cosponsor (1 of 50 Senate Republicans), but the bill never came to a vote in either chamber, so no roll-call shows where the parties actually stood.

industries.note: The bill bans issuers from locking transactions into the two largest networks, directly attacking the Visa–Mastercard duopoly's routing share and the fee income that comes with it. Their loss is the merchant savings the bill is built to create.

industries.industry: Large banks and card issuers (over $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: Interchange fees fund a large slice of these banks' card revenue; routing competition would pressure those fees downward. They argued the lost revenue would ultimately be recovered from cardholders through rewards and fees.

industries.industry: Merchants and retailers, large and small
industries.note: Merchants pay a swipe fee on every credit card sale; the bill lets them route each sale to the cheapest eligible network and bars penalties for doing so. Their savings could translate into lower prices for shoppers.
The bill exempts cards issued by a network itself, leaving American Express and Discover's closed-loop fee model entirely untouched while their two big competitors face routing mandates.

industries.industry: Community banks and credit unions (under $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: They are explicitly exempt from the routing mandate, but their co-branded cards ride on the same networks as big banks' cards, and they argued they would still lose fee and rewards revenue as large-issuer cards shift routing.
